Variants.Content: Blackport City is located on the western frontier of the Stormlands and is the traditional territory of the Dondarrion family. It is far away from the Dorne Passage and the busy water network of the Riverlands, relying on mountain roads, pastures, woodlands and border knights who can dispatch quickly. The "blackness" of Black Harbor is more of a color left by the landscape and the old name, which does not mean that the place will always be dark; what truly shapes the residents is the caution of frontier society - every strange team may be a merchant, a refugee or a plunderer. The coat of arms and vassal obligations of House Dondarrion connect this place to the larger politics of the Stormlands, but local life still revolves around wells, livestock, and watchtowers.

Entry Blackhaven Local families also depend on rainforest timber, game, barren farmland, fisheries, and roofs to protect themselves from storms; any time a road, well, or dock fails, the price falls first on them.

Entry Blackhaven They also recognize the accents, laws, and credentials of the Stormlands; reputations can travel great distances from taverns, but true distances must still be measured by wheel, oar, or horse's hoof.

Entry Blackhaven If you can supply supplies, avoid danger, and find a guide, it is worth marking in your itinerary; if you don't have these three things, no matter how loud your family name is, it won't be able to save the lost.

The traces left by generations of people in Blackport City are half hidden in the boats, bridges, millstones, fishing nets and riverside churches, and half are hidden in the old history of the Seven Gods, the Storm King and the thick stone walls that resist the sea breeze. A stronghold was therefore not just a lord's hall, but also a place where weddings and funerals, vows, labor and local memories recurred.

Entry Blackhaven They care about rainforest timber, prey, barren farmland, fish catches, and roofs to shelter from storms. They also look at whether seeds are left after harvesting grain, and whether the city gates are open in times of disaster. When people from afar see coats of arms, what they see is whether there will be food to eat tomorrow.
